episode_title: The Power of High Agency, PM Skills, and Career Frameworks
guest_role: Former Product Leader at Stripe, Twitter, Yahoo, and Google
content:
Lenny: Shreyas, you popularized the concept of 'High Agency' in product management. How do you define High Agency, and why is it the single greatest predictor of PM success?

Shreyas Doshi: High agency is the quality of bending reality to what you want to achieve, rather than accepting the boundaries presented to you. When you give a task to a low-agency person and they encounter an obstacle—a blocked API, a missing budget, an uncooperative stakeholder—they come back and say 'I couldn't do it because X happened.' When you give that exact same situation to a high-agency person, they find a way. They negotiate, they rethink the scope, they discover an unpaved workaround, or they align incentives so everyone wins.

Lenny: You also introduced the LNO framework for time management for busy product managers. Can you break that down?

Shreyas Doshi: Most PMs are overwhelmed because they treat all tasks as equally important. In product management, tasks fall into three buckets: L, N, and O.

1. 'L' stands for Leverage tasks. These are things where doing an exceptional 10x job creates disproportionate impact for the business or team. Examples include defining the core product strategy, hiring an exceptional anchor engineer, or running a game-changing customer research interview. On L tasks, you must invest extreme care and push for perfection.

2. 'N' stands for Neutral tasks. These are standard expectations. If you do them well, things run smoothly. If you do them poorly, things break, but doing them at 10x perfection yields almost zero extra ROI. Examples: weekly sprint status updates, reviewing standard PRDs, standard cross-functional syncs. Do them at a good, competent level and move on quickly.

3. 'O' stands for Overhead tasks. These are low-value operational chores: filling out compliance questionnaires, scheduling repetitive meetings, trivial admin work. On O tasks, your goal should be to do them as fast as possible, delegate them, or automate them.

If you spend 80% of your energy on L tasks and aggressively cap your time on N and O tasks, your trajectory as a product leader will skyrocket.
